content.entityName: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

data.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
data.summary: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn't stay private.
data.content: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. content.entityName: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI

data.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
data.summary: Researcher finds 35,000 Grok Build apps wide open to anyone who looked for them.
data.content: Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it. You had one job Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals. content.entityName: Nintendo's biggest ROM chip supplier is bowing out of the business

data.title: Nintendo's biggest ROM chip supplier is bowing out of the business
data.summary: And what that could mean for physical Switch game costs.
data.content: For years, the AI industry's insatiable demand for memory and storage has had plenty of knock-on effects on the price and availability of PC components like RAM , SSDs , and GPUs . Now those shortages are also squeezing the supply of ROM chips that power physical Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 game cartridges. Chip manufacturer Macronix announced in its third-quarter earnings report that the company's production of ROM chips "has reached its end" and that it will begin "gradually decoupling from the game industry," as reported by Taiwanese news site BigGo Finance . That could be an issue for Nintendo, which, analyst David Gibson notes, uses Macronix as its "main memory chip maker" for physical game cartridges. That ROM production—which has shrunk 39 percent in the last year and now represents just 5 percent of Macronix's business—is being crowded out by production of more lucrative in-demand chips like NOR- and NAND-based memory and eMMCs, the company said. With Macronix's production capacity stuck at 25,000 12-inch wafers a month—and $1.2 billion in planned new capacity taking a year or more to spin up—less profitable ROM chips are taking up wafer space that can earn more through other types of chips. data.title: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections

data.content: If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden's win that November. If you ask Google's AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources. When I put the direct question of "Who won the 2020 presidential election?" to Google's AI Mode this morning (after seeing complaints about cagey answers on social media ), I got the following surprisingly indirect response: "To review the official results and statistics of the 2020 United States presidential election, including the final electoral college breakdown, popular vote counts, and winner certification, please consult the official report compiled by the Federal Election Commission (FEC)." data.title: Vibe genes? Natural(ish) language comes to protein, genome design software
data.summary: You can apparently now tell AI tools what sort of protein you want them to make.
data.content: Protein design tools may be getting increasingly sophisticated , but you still need a sophisticated understanding of protein structure for them to work. This can include knowing enzyme mechanisms down to the positions of specific amino acids, as well as the water molecules that also occupy the area where catalysis takes place. Once you specify these, the tools can build the rest of a protein around this target. A large collaboration of researchers based in China, however, decided to bring protein design to the masses, making a tool that can take natural language prompts and use them to produce proteins with the function you specify. If your measure for success is a working protein, then the success rate may not be great. But they still manage to get the job done. And, in a separate announcement, Hugging Face shared that it's now hosting a tool that does similar things on the DNA level. The equivalent of vibe coding may have come to protein design—at least if you have access to a lab where you can sort the good designs from the dozens of failed ones. Read full article Comments

content.entityName: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins

data.title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
data.summary: AI design tools make proteins that break bonds that are stable for hundreds of years.
data.content: A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they're estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth's environment, most proteins don't last nearly that long. That's because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment. Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases. Cutting proteins The basic peptide bond isn't especially interesting-looking—it's what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.) content.entityName: OpenAI will watermark ChatGPT outputs by default—but only in the EU

data.title: OpenAI will watermark ChatGPT outputs by default—but only in the EU
data.summary: Like other solutions, it is not especially reliable, and it's easy to circumvent.
data.content: OpenAI will begin automatically watermarking text generated with ChatGPT in the European Union, the company has announced. It will also offer the watermarking feature in other regions, but it will be off by default outside of the EU. The move in Europe is driven by a need to comply with the EU AI Act, which took effect in August. It requires marking content produced by AI models in a way that another tool can detect. Unfortunately, there is still no completely effective and reliable way to do that. A few standards already exist, like SynthID and the C2PA project, but they are relatively easy to circumvent for anyone with basic know-how. The same is likely true for OpenAI's watermark. Its method is proprietary; the company calls it textGrain, and has published a technical paper explaining how it works. But in general, it works like other LLM watermarking tools we've seen in the past: It puts patterns in the word choices that are not clear to a human reader and that don't meaningfully change the general quality of the output, but that someone with a key can use a specialized detector to find. OpenAI says it will be giving access to the detector to a limited number of researchers and organizations and providing a request-for-approval process for others to be added over time. content.entityName: With most information hidden, the game Stratego had stumped AI—until now

data.title: With most information hidden, the game Stratego had stumped AI—until now
data.summary: Adding in a second neural network that guesses the identity of hidden pieces was key.
data.content: Deep Blue took down Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997, AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol at Go in 2016, and poker bots have been beating professionals for years. But one classic game called Stratego held out. Even DeepMind, with its exceptional budget, couldn't build a machine that reliably beat the best human players. Now, a team of researchers from Carnegie Mellon, MIT, New York University, and Stanford University has done it. Their AI, called Ataraxos, beat Pim Niemeijer, arguably the best Stratego player of all time, 15 games to one, with four draws. And it took just 16 GPUs and a few thousand dollars to train it. Hidden armies In Stratego , each player gets 40 pieces representing military ranks, from a marshal down to a spy, plus bombs and a flag. You win by capturing the opponent's flag. Your opponent knows where your pieces are, but not what they are. Identities are revealed only when two pieces collide in battle—the weaker one is removed, and the identity of the winner is revealed. That makes Stratego an imperfect-information game, just like poker, which computers cracked years ago. “There's something super distinctive about Stratego , which is that it is a massive amount of hidden information that unfolds over a very long time scale,” said Eugene Vinitsky, a researcher at NYU and co-author of the study. content.entityName: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update

data.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
data.summary: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely…
data.content: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work. It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development. And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement. METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research. In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance. Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.” Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August , he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite. Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down. Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category. But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.” Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].” In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task. In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming. It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”

data.content: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack . You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

content.entityName: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s

data.title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
data.summary: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation…
data.content: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases. Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science. OSMO AI A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary. Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.) The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later. Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes. But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows , has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack , arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. In response, Wiltschko says that “human perception isn’t a workaround for AI”. “Language models learn from what people have written. Our model learns from what people smell. Smell is ultimately a human experience, so the model has to learn from humans to bridge chemistry and perception. That’s what lets it predict how people will experience a scent as well as the human nose does.” Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since. But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.” In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies . For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize. “There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.” This article has been updated with an additional comment from Alex Wiltschko.

content.entityName: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back

data.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
data.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia…
data.content: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress. On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell. But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good. The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

content.entityName: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it

data.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
data.summary: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do…
data.content: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence. Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside. Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox. With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned. Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event. Building trust that scales It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest. Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark. The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do. Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions: What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution. Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds. Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step. Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows. Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle. The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption. Explore how UL Solutions builds trust in AI . This content was produced by UL Solutions. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

content.entityName: Building AI that can work across the enterprise

data.title: Building AI that can work across the enterprise
data.summary: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance,…
data.content: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says. Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit. Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond. This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys. Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. This episode is produced in partnership with Infosys. Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we’re still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI’s value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It’s becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can’t simply be added into an enterprise’s existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what’s inside and how it’s used. Two words for you: conscious configuration. My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy. Welcome, Thorsten and Satinder. Thorsten Leiduck: Yeah, thank you for having us. Really a pleasure to be here with our valued partner, Infosys. Looking forward to the conversation. Satinder Pal Singh: Hi, Megan. Thanks for inviting for the conversation today. Looking forward to the discussion. Megan: Me too. Thank you both so much for being here. Thorsten, if I could start with you. We know that many senior leaders understand the transformative potential in AI, but they continue to struggle with aspects of its implementation. Many projects remain stuck at a pilot phase, for example. When you speak to clients, what are the biggest obstacles they face when it comes to integrating AI into their tech stack? Thorsten: Yeah. Megan, as you mentioned, AI is on the agenda of every client conversation today, but many customers are really struggling how to convert that interest into an operationalized model and to unlock the value of AI across the enterprise. And the reason is that too many programs start as isolated POCs on different AI technologies and in an inconsistent fragmented data foundation. This creates a lot of duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale. At the same time, leaders are highly concerned about security, observability, reliability of agents, and some ethical implications when those get deployed. This is also shown in some studies. For example, BCG has launched a report, which shows that 74% of the organizations are stuck in pilot mode with no plan to scale. And in an Anthropic survey, data said that 42% are really struggling with getting access to the data and the quality to really, basically, scale the entire AI capabilities across the organization. The path forward is really to treat AI not just as a project, but more holistically, as an enterprise platform, one that really consistently connects an unified data layer with the process context of the applications, and then embed AI capabilities governed across the entire life cycle. And to make this real, we in SAP launched the SAP autonomous enterprise framework, so organizations can move from pilots to scaled outcomes. Megan: Yeah, really, to provide that support. And, Satinder, would you agree, why is it that we’re seeing enterprises get a touch of almost AI paralysis here? What’s the mindset shift that needs to happen and, perhaps, why is this something organizations need to be thinking about now, as well? Satinder: Absolutely, Megan. And, if anything, the picture sharpens when you look at, specifically, at agentic AI. Infosys and HFS research surveyed over 500 global 2,000 enterprises and found only 14% have successfully scaled AI. Eighty-six percent remain in early exploration, proof of concept, or fragmented pilot phases. For a technology at the top of every boardroom agenda for two years, that’s a striking failure rate. And at the core of that 86% is what I would describe as AI as a department trap. What happens is that an organization creates an AI team or a center of excellence and walls it off from business. That team builds technically excellent pilots the business doesn’t recognize itself in, and you end up with AI solutions searching for problems, rather than the other way around. Mindset shift is clear. Move from treating AI as a technology initiative to treating it as an operating model transformation. AI stops being something IT does for business and starts being something the whole organization does together. Every function, every workflow, embedded from the start. And what makes this a now problem? Early movers are building an advantage. You cannot close by buying the same platform later. Eighteen months of agent behavior data, calibrated knowledge graph, workforce that has genuinely internalized AI, that is a structural advantage that compounds. Infosys Knowledge Institute AI Maturity Index shows that only 8% of the companies qualify as AI native today, yet they achieve four times the revenue contribution from the AI versus laggards. If you’re not building AI today, you’re not standing still, you’re falling behind at an accelerating rate. Megan: Right. There’s a real polarization there, isn’t there, between the front-runners and the laggards, as you say. As we shift from pilot to scaled-up applications, perhaps the first step is evaluating when AI is the right tool. AI has quickly become the default solution within many enterprises. Is there a tendency to use it as a bit of a blunt instrument, nowadays, Thorsten? At the outset, how can senior leaders better evaluate what use cases are worthy of their time and investment, in order to strip out some of that later complexity? Thorsten: Yeah, I think, Megan, what everybody needs to be aware is adopting and rolling out AI across an organization is as much a change management journey as it’s a technology rollout. Now, when you have this in mind, it makes absolutely sense to put AI in front as many teams as possible, because you want to build formality, and spark ideas, and also people should see the benefit of AI in an organization. When you think about travel assistance, meeting summaries via Copilot, or AI-enabled workflows, increase the productivity, everybody feels this in their real job, in their real daily business. And, obviously, this creates creativity and also provides the organization from a bottom-up perspective with some innovation scale. Now, however, as majority grows, the conversation, and this is also what we discuss with many of the leaders, and our clients, shifts more to economics and governance. Things like token costs, model performance, security, and accountability become much more relevant. And when you then take the approach and think about AI agents as digital workers that execute specific tasks within a business process, then this means, from an AI perspective, not every task justifies nation. In some cases, human effort remains more economical or effective. The smart approach, and that’s what we really recommend to our clients, is to start with a defined, maybe small set of high-value use cases with defined success metrics upfront. So, for example, such as cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, or cost of per transaction, or top line improvement, and then scale what works. Those use cases can be tied to a line of business domains or industry scenarios. And then, what we are doing from an SAP perspective, together with Infosys, we really help customers to be successful. We provide, as part of our autonomous suite, the according domain assistance, which really run business processes end-to-end and which deliver find ROIs for single end-to-end business process steps. And then, last but not least, in many scenarios, I think, which has been very common pattern in particular around large industry AI use cases, is a joint approach, and we do this with partners like Infosys, but also customers around forward deployed engineering, so that you really define very closely the AI-specific use case with the defined outcomes together with the customer, and deliver this as the initial projects. And then, ideally, scale this to other customers and take it back like a best practice, which can be rolled out to other organizations, as well. Megan: Right. It’s been really clear, isn’t it, on what you’re looking to achieve and what’s worth your time, as I say. And what would your advice, Satinder, be here, on refining an AI strategy to ensure organizations can focus on those areas, where AI can deliver the highest returns? Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten’s framing of AI agents as digital coworkers forces a precision that agentic AI strategy language often lacks. When you ask which digital coworkers do we need and where do they deliver the most value, the answer starts to become clearer right from the first step. At Infosys, through our Topaz AI-first framework, we push clients through the three lenses simultaneously. The first one is impact. Where does deploying an agent move the numbers that matter? Revenue, cost, working capital risk. We have built a library of over 300 enterprise use cases across industries, so we never begin from a blank page. The second is feasibility. Given your data foundation platform and talent today, which high-impact use cases can you actually execute? Feasibility determines your sequence. The high-impact use case on a broken data foundation is not viable. When the foundation is right, the results are dramatic. One Infosys engagement cut complex SAP-specification documents from 86 person hours to 6, a 92% reduction. Third is scalability. Once you have proven a use case with clear ROI metrics, cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, cost per transaction, what’s the architecture that lets you replicate it? A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment. My practical advice: treat your AI portfolio like an investment portfolio, quick wins that fund the program, medium-term bets, one or two bold, long-term positions that balance keep stakeholders engaged at every stage and not just in year three. Megan: That’s such a useful framework for people to use there. And given the urgency here, Thorsten, how can organizations approach and manage AI in a more structured, efficient way? To start with, what are the fundamentals that some organizations perhaps miss at the moment? I know Infosys and SAP talk about platform and data, then AI, for example. Thorsten: Yeah, Megan, I think the fundamental, which many organizations are overlooking, is data and the data is a foundation for AI. Because, at the end, without the data structures and the ability to access the right information at the right time and basically bringing different kind of structured, unstructured data sources together, in a meaningful governed and semantic way, there will be no successful AI. AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation. And I think this is often overlooked, and that’s why I said when you start POCs in different organization, or different parts of the organization with different technologies, it’s very hard to establish an end-to-end consistent model on the data side, as well as on the AI side. One of the key goals companies need to achieve is, and that’s why we really talk about you need to start with data first and the platform first, is to establish and semantically-rich connected data layer that really reflects your business, so that the agents are really grounded in the company’s reality and not just in generic patterns. And then, I think, the second element that’s important is accuracy. In the enterprise context, it really matters. For example, what might pass in a consumer setting, where you have 80% accuracy, and even in a workforce environment where you build PowerPoints or you do email drafts, which you then, with a human in the loop, optimize, 80% might be good enough. But, when you really think about mission-critical or business-critical processes in the supply chain, or closing the books, 80% is a very terrible result. The stakes are much too high and you need to have much more accuracy. And that’s why it’s important that you have business process logic and industry context embedded into the data and the models which build the foundation, if you will, the backbone for every AI and, obviously, for the data in the ERP and the line of business system. And then, last but not least, the other critical element, and you see this obviously in the news with all the agents going rogue, are governance, compliance, and security. Very critical in an enterprise context. You need to set clear policies, access controls. You need to have monitoring ability, capabilities, to really make sure that what then the AI agenda capabilities or agents are executing is fully aligned, is trustworthy, and scalable. Megan: Right. Which is quite a lot of things for organizations to be thinking about. Satinder, how do SAP and Infosys work with organizations to streamline some of these processes, perhaps and make unlocking AI’s capability a little bit easier? Satinder: Megan, I think at the onset, I want to acknowledge that, at Infosys, we are uniquely positioned for our relationship with SAP, because we are a customer to SAP, as well as one of their key global suppliers. And the way SAP and Infosys work together is designed around the architecture Thorsten described, that defines a coherent partnership. SAP brings the platform foundation, business data cloud for the semantically-rich enterprise, generative AI hub for governed LLMXs, and agent hub for the lifecycle governance, enterprise grade from day one. Infosys brings implementation depth, industry context, and use case accelerators. Through Infosys Topaz, we have built over 50 pre-configured AI use cases on Business AI Platform, production-ready configurations deployable without building from scratch. We co-develop use cases within SAP’s industry AI engagement with clear customer-specific FTE metrics. That shared accountability for results is different from a typical implementation engagement. In practice, one global S/4HANA transformation program used AI-assisted delivery tooling to complete over 480 RICEF objects in five months, a pace conventional delivery would not sustain. In another account, an AI-powered platform auto-classifies over 120,000 SAP incidents monthly, with zero analyst charge. The combined effect time to value drops from 12 to 18 months, down to four to six months. What I would emphasize is change management damage. Technology is increasingly deployable, and Thorsten also spoke about it earlier. What’s hard is helping an organization internalize that their agents are digital coworkers, not automations . That mindset shift is 70% of the implementation challenge that platform cannot solve alone, and Infosys and SAP run joint adoption programs addressing both the dimensions in parallel. Megan: Fantastic. Some great real-world examples there, as well. Thorsten, can you tell us a little bit more about SAP’s Business AI Platform, or BAIP, in particular? How does that work and what sets it apart from other platforms? Thorsten: Yeah, so SAP Business AI Platform, if you will, is the foundation for our SAP autonomous enterprise framework, which really consists of a unified user interface and is enabled as an agentic orchestration layer, which we call Joule. And you have the autonomous read with all the applications, and then you have the Business AI Platform, which powers the other capabilities, and is closely connected, and is basically organized around three core pillars. The first one is, really, what we call build. What it means is you provide the respective intent-based development tools, so that customer, or partners like Infosys, can really create and development agents, applications and workflows using best-in-class tools and model to extend SAP’s own assistant, or customizing those, or really building own agents as needed. Complimenting what Satinder said, it’s really critical for us that we have a thriving ecosystem, who is innovative, and is building innovations, and is complementing our own SAP agentic portfolio. We are focusing on specific areas on the domains, from a line of business industry perspective, where we deliver assistance as part of our organization, but to really then customize them from a last mile execution from really complimenting areas which we don’t cover and really driving the innovation towards the customer, our ecosystem is the multiplier force and Infosys is really playing a leading role here with us, together. Second is, and we talked about this, is what we call the contextualize and reason pillar, which is literally as a foundation data, we address with SAP Data Cloud and comprehensive data strategy, where we establish an end-to-end data fabric across partner provider platforms, like Databricks, Snowflakes, where we promote and zero copy access to data. For the customer, this is very important. So, we allow, basically, promote to customers if you have made investments in any of those platforms, reserve those investments and just leverage BDC to connect without moving data around your, for example, Databricks, Snowflake environment to BDC. With this approach, we establish and harmonize semantic data layer, which can then be used for any AI scenario across the entire enterprise, combining different data sources without any disruption. The other key element that’s part of this is the generative AI hub. We have aggregated more than 50 models, language models, including some of our own models into it, in single cockpit, so that customers can access and choose any of those 50 models as part of the generative-AI hub, which is part of the platform. And then, as a key differentiator, we really moved a lot of business semantic and context into the knowledge graph, which then helps to navigate the agents and acts like a nerve, or navigation system, in the company to really provide business-relevant, customer-specific information for the decision making and the execution to any agentic execution framework. And then, we talked about governance, last but not least. This is the third pillar, which is very critical and this is built-in. So, we have, as the third pillar, the SAP agent hub, which is kind of a command center for enterprise-wide AI and agent governments. You can govern SAP agents, you can also govern non-SAP agents, as long as they’re integrating to SAP via A2A. So, the team can really manage, on the customer side, an end-to-end life cycle of agents and features from hire to retire. Megan: Fantastic. That’s a really comprehensive overview. Thank you ever so much. And, Satinder, can you share any examples, perhaps, of how organizations have used SAP Business AI Platform in practice, to improve the ways they’ve used AI? Perhaps, what was the challenge they faced, what did the process look like, and what benefits did they unlock? Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten just explained how powerful a platform Business AI Platform is. And this is decades in working. We also have been using that, and I’ll share two examples from live Infosys engagements, both showing what BIP’s three pillar look like in production. The first is global diversified manufacturer with a large SAP estate. The challenge was month-end close, 80-plus SAP transaction codes, period closed teams working nights and weekends, L1 support absorbing over 300 incidents per month, from close cycle alone. On Business AI Platform, we deployed Topaz Fabric, Infosys’ agentic orchestration platform, with a master agent coordinating five specialist child agents, WBS accrual, revenue recognition, intercompany settlement, master data reconciliation, and SOX audit trail generation. Agents run autonomously, escalating to humans only for genuine exceptions. The result, entire L1.5 support tier eliminated, over 300 monthly incidents handled with zero human touch. The close team redeployed from reactive firefighting to forward-looking financial analysis. Annual savings pipeline exceed $1 million. The second is North American Utility in a S/4HANA transformation. Their challenge was development velocity, complex SAP functional specification documents routinely requiring 80 or more personnel each, a bottleneck throttling the entire program. Using AI native development environment on Business AI Platform with a Claude-powered retrieval system, we reduced those specifications from 86 hours to six, a 92% reduction, validated across 51 SAP task types at 95% accuracy. The architecture is now being replicated across accounts. In both cases, the pattern matches what Thorsten described, governed data foundation, SAP business process context, full agent observability through SAP Agent Hub. That’s the autonomous enterprise running as daily operations, not as a concept. Megan: And those are some really compelling concrete results I think would be really helpful for people to hear. Also, of course, responsible AI, or clear governance frameworks, are a critical component of AI integration, too. And we know that tools like LLMs are rarely developed with compliance built-in. I wonder what’s your advice there, Thorsten, on how to ensure that property governance is embedded into an ERP? Thorsten: Yeah, I mean, Megan, you’re absolutely right. Governance compliance and security are really mission-critical to delivering relevant, reliable, and trustworthy AI at enterprise scale. I mean, it’s important to understand how in public LLM service really works. Many of those services are trained on internet scale data, which means they’re public models. Depending on the provider’s policies and setting, they may retain easier inputs for model improvement, which means if a company provides data back to the model, this company data is in the public domain. For example, pipeline information or forecast information, which is becoming very, very critical, because this exposes your organization, really, at significant risk. So, while then LLMs X are really great, imposes in large volumes of text and other unstructured data, they are less effective with structured tables like in EOP systems, or in business applications, in general, and then they’re lacking, usually, the nuance of business process and logic and context. That’s why a robust governance framework is essential. We talked about the generative AI, how we aggregate those models in a single cockpit. And then, the other element, which we previously touched based on and Satinder mentioned, is always a part of the custom examples is SAP agent hub or, in general, when we talk about the capabilities just in AI lifecycle governance, which really includes agent registry, LMN registries, MCP registry, so a single source of tool for every AI artifact that you can manage identity and access control, so that agents are really variable and that you can really provide the right permissions, in terms of which agents allowed to use access which data, and then agent observability, agent minus, and then also map the agent skills to the organization is very critical. As all of part of this, as I mentioned before, we provide those capabilities really fully embedded into the Business AI Platform to really provide this governance framework out of the box and fully embedded into everything what you do at SAP. Megan: Which is so important, because when organizations are experimenting with, or scaling up multiple AI programs and tools, in some cases, it adds real complexity. I wonder, Satinder, would you add anything on how organizations can have that robust layer of governance built in, even with a pretty complex tech stack? Satinder: We, at Infosys, have our Infosys Knowledge Institute, they run this annual magazine generative AI radar, and it found that 48% of companies had deployed generative AI without a formal governance policy. Nearly half of the enterprises were running AI with no documented framework or oversight, accountability, or compliance. That’s the gap that Thorsten is describing, and it has to be closed proactively before an incident forces a reactive stop or audit far more disruptive than building a governance upfront. What Thorsten has just described in SAP Agent Hub is exactly the platform layer that makes enterprise-wide governance possible and is worth making the overall architecture explicit, because without it, governance is theoretical. The framework I use with clients has three layers that have to work together. The first one is policy, a clear organization-wide AI use policy, what agents can and cannot do autonomously, how data can be used for AI training, disclosure obligations, and accountability for outcomes. This needs legal, compliance, technology teams together with a board level sponsorship. Without that foundation, every deployment becomes an ad hoc governance debate. Second layer is platform. This is where SAP Business AI Platform and, specifically, SAP Agent Hub becomes enterprise control tower. The capabilities Thorsten described, agent LLM, MCP registry as a single source of truth, verifiable agent identities with scoped access trails, agent observability, agent mining for drift detection, these aren’t just governance features. They give leaders real-time visibility across a complex multi-agent landscape. You can see what’s running, what it’s consuming, and whether it’s performing as expected. That’s what turns a complex tech stack from a governance liability to a governance asset. And the last layer is process, the recurring governance rituals, quarterly AI risk reviews, bias audit cycles, model performance reviews against the business KPIs, these structured conversations that keep humans accountable for the agent behavior over time. What organizations consistently discover is that this three-layer structure actually accelerates the deployment. Every new use case has a clear path through approval and a governance architecture to plug into. The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption. It creates a risk backlog that eventually forces a stop and audit movement far more disruptive than building the governance muscle. Megan: That’s such an interesting point. Thank you so much for that. And we’ve covered a lot of ground, so to close with a future forward look, we’ve spoken today about the proliferation of AI tools that are now on the market, many designed to transform enterprise-level operations. I wonder, what do you see on the horizon, Thorsten, that you think could be a real game-changer? Thorsten: I think what we will see very soon, and we talked about this briefly, is that we are heading into a period of sustained, rapid AI adoption, where assistance and agents will operate as digital coworkers. They will be embedded in our organizations like employees today, and they will be embedded into processes as people perform tasks, as we speak. Now, as this happens, the Center of Gravity will shift more and more from a monolithic application layer to an agentic value layer that orchestrates work across systems and across different landscapes, which need to be orchestrated very well. I think what we also will see, and this will be likely, at least in terms of scale, I believe a game-changer, is that the delivery will become industrialized. When you think about agent factories and church services that really design, test, and govern agents at scale, or you can say agentic frameworks at scale, and I think we will see an evolution of commercial models, which are today more consumption-based towards really value and outcome-based agreements, which are then tied to clear business KPIs. On the technology front, I think there’s still so much movement on the LLM landscape, new architectures, training methods. I think we’ll bring down, significantly, the total cost of ownership, while also control and the viability will be improved. I think there’s an awareness which the recent examples in the market show, and then I think the innovation will be playable. And I think the big question is, from that perspective, which role is China going to play in a global context, and also how those models are really embedded. Last but not least, most importantly, even I think ontology and customer-specific knowledge graphs will become first-class assets, and I think this will be the key differentiation in the future, because they will lead in code process, semantics, policies, what Satinder talked about, and data relationships. And they are the blueprint for secure high-performing enterprise agent architectures in the future. Megan: Which is, of course, what we’re aiming for. And how about you, Satinder? What would you flag as a really exciting area of development? Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think what excites me most is the shift from AI as productivity tool to AI as a decision-making partner. The most important evolution Thorsten’s architecture makes possible. For decades, enterprise systems have told us what happened. The next generation helps leader understand what is happening now, what will happen next, what actions to take. The scenario I keep coming back to, a CFO starting a day with an agent that continuously analyzes signals across finance, supply chain, procurement, workforce data, proactively surfacing the three issues that are most likely to impact the quarter, with recommended actions, financial impact quantified. That’s not a dashboard. That’s a fundamentally different decision model. Through Infosys Topaz, we are helping clients move forward an AI-first enterprise, one that can sense, learn, decide, adapt continuously across the different domains. What also excites me is the pace of AI evolution. In past technology waves, constraints were stable. You identify a limitation and architect around it for years. AI is different. Use cases that appear constrained at program start are often resolved before go live. SAP’s prior model transformed structured data reasoning once a clear LLM gap. Decision intelligence is arriving faster than most organization are planning for. The winning strategy is to design for where AI will be 18 months from now, flexible architecture, trusted data foundation, governance that absorbs innovation as it arrives. Organizations that do this compound value at each new generation of capabilities becomes available. So, the next frontier isn’t that AI can do more work. It’s that AI that understands your business well enough to help you make better decision. And that’s where the greatest opportunity for SAP, Infosys, and our clients lies, convergence of systems of record with systems of intelligence. Megan: Fantastic. Certainly, lots on the horizon to look forward to. Thank you both so much for joining us today. That was Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America at SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England. That’s it for this episode of Business Lab. I’m your host, Megan Tatum. I’m a contributing editor and host for Insights, the custom publishing division of MIT Technology Review. We were founded in 1899 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and you can find us in print, on the web, and at events each year around the world. For more information about us and the show, please check out our website, thetechnologyreview.com. This show is available wherever you get your podcasts. And if you enjoyed this episode, we hope you’ll take a moment to rate and review us. Business Lab is a production of MIT Technology Review, and this episode was produced by Giro Studios. Thank you so much for listening. Goodbye. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.
