content.entityName: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility

data.title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
data.summary: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on…
data.content: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers. The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified. In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

data.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
data.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where…
data.content: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport . Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that. But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something. So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia. But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

content.entityName: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI

data.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
data.summary: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a…
data.content: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says. And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.” He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk. “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.” Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI. But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

content.entityName: Baseten Releases Bison-1 and Groundhog-1, Topping Decision Model Index

data.title: Baseten Releases Bison-1 and Groundhog-1, Topping Decision Model Index
data.summary: Baseten released bison-1 and groundhog-1, open-weight decision models built on Gemma 4. bison-1 scores 76 on the AA Decision Index v2.1, and both models support 128k context and image input. The post Baseten Releases Bison-1 and Groundhog-1, Topping Decision Model Index appeared first on MarkTechPost .
data.content:
Baseten has released bison-1 and groundhog-1, 2 open-weight decision models built on Google’s Gemma 4 . Decision models do not write text. They return calibrated probabilities for yes/no, choice and score questions. The Baseten bison-1 decision model scores 76 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 . That ranks #1 of 19. Both models raise context from 16k to 128k tokens and accept images. For routing, triage and guardrail pipelines, that means full policies and histories in one call. TL;DR Size: bison-1 is 31B dense. groundhog-1 is a 26B MoE with about 4B active. Both take 128k tokens (131,072). Runs on: Baseten Model APIs, plus open BF16 weights on Hugging Face. No inference GPU or quantized builds are listed. BF16 weights alone are about 62 GB (bison-1) and 52 GB (groundhog-1), by our arithmetic. Performance: bison-1 scores 76 on AA Decision Index v2.1, 1 point above Liquid AI’s d1.2-ultra (75). Best: When2Call, 98 (rank #1). Worst: AA-Omniscience-Decision v1.1, 60 (rank #11). Bottom line: Best: top-ranked, best-calibrated decisions (Brier 0.14) over 128k tokens at $0.10 per 1M input tokens. Worst: groundhog-1 has no official index score yet, and every number is self-reported. What are bison-1 and groundhog-1? bison-1 is a 31B decision model from Baseten that post-trains Gemma 4 31B to return calibrated probabilities. groundhog-1 is the cheaper sibling. It fine-tunes Gemma 4 26B-A4B , a mixture-of-experts model with about 4B active parameters per token. Both join Baseten’s existing lineup: mammoth-1 (27B), elephant-1 (9B) and joey-1 (2B). Those 3 sit on Qwen backbones. The new pair is Baseten’s first on what it calls an American backbone. How does a decision model work? A request carries 1 state and any number of questions . The state is text, optionally with images. Each question has a type: noul (yes/no), choice (named options) or score (ordered levels). The model answers every question in a single prefill pass. It returns P(yes), or the chosen option with a probabilities field. No output tokens are generated. Baseten’s earlier launch post lists ticket triage, spam detection, jailbreak guardrails and LLM routing as target tasks. Requests longer than the trained limit are refused, not truncated. Pipelines that assume silent truncation will need a length check. Why is bison-1 better calibrated? Baseten credits two sources: the Gemma base and more “soft labels” in the training mix. Soft labels use probability targets instead of 1 fixed correct answer. The model learns to report uncertainty that tracks how often it is right. The result is a Brier score of 0.14, the lowest on the index. Baseten puts d1.2-ultra at 0.15. Lower is better. How does bison-1 score on benchmarks? On AA Decision Index v2.1, bison-1 scores 76. Liquid AI’s d1.2-ultra scores 75 and mammoth-1 scores 71. The index blends 6 evaluations, led by AA-Paperclip at 30%. The bison-1 model card breaks out each component: When2Call: 98 (#1) EvalSafe-O*NET-AA: 93 (#1) AA-Symmetry v1.1: 89 (#1) AA-Paperclip: 73 (#2) HLE-MultiChoice v1.1: 51 (#1) AA-Omniscience-Decision v1.1: 60 (#11) bison-1 ranks first on 4 of 6 components. Knowledge-heavy decisions are its weak spot. On long context, Baseten reports LongMemEval M (128k) of 84.8 for bison-1 and 77.4 for groundhog-1. LongMemEval S reads 87.1 and 79.3. groundhog-1 has no official index score yet. Baseten expects it to match mammoth-1. Auto-play

content.entityName: RadixArk Ships DaisyRose-27B, a 27B Agentic Coding Model Trained With Reinforcement Learning Only

data.title: RadixArk Ships DaisyRose-27B, a 27B Agentic Coding Model Trained With Reinforcement Learning Only
data.summary: RadixArk released DaisyRose-27B, an Apache 2.0 agentic coding model post-trained from Qwen3.8-27B with reinforcement learning only. It more than doubles Terminal Bench 4.1 pass@1 to 12.0 and runs on a single GPU. The post RadixArk Ships DaisyRose-27B, a 27B Agentic Coding Model Trained With Reinforcement Learning Only appeared first on MarkTechPost .
data.content:
This week RadixArk released DaisyRose-27B , its first open-weight model. DaisyRose-27B is an agentic coding model from RadixArk, post-trained from Qwen3.8-27B with reinforcement learning (RL). The model card page states that it used RL only, with no SFT or distillation. It ships under Apache 2.0 as a drop-in replacement for the base model. The main result: Terminal Bench 4.1 pass@1 rises from 5.6 to 12.0. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 27.8B dense parameters (0.46B vision encoder, 0.42B MTP head), 262,144-token context. Runs on: 1 GPU. BF16 is about 52 GB, FP8 about 29 GB, NVFP4 about 23 GB (Blackwell only). Listed targets: H200, B200, GB300, RTX PRO 6000, RTX 5090, DGX Spark. GGUF also available. Performance: Beats its Qwen3.8-27B base on all 7 reported benchmarks. Best: IFBench 82.4, the top score among the 9 models RadixArk compared. Worst: HLE (text only) 34.3, only +0.4 over the base and below Inkling 2 Small’s 44.1. Bottom line: Best: Terminal Bench 4.1 more than doubles after 18 days of RL. Worst: it still trails much larger MoE models on hard agentic tasks. What is DaisyRose-27B? DaisyRose-27B keeps the Qwen3.8-27B architecture unchanged. The model card lists 64 decoder layers in a 3:1 pattern. Three Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers alternate with 1 full-attention layer. Hidden size is 5,120. A 27-layer vision encoder handles images. One multi-token-prediction layer supports speculative decoding. Input is text and images, output is text, and it is a thinking model. How was DaisyRose-27B trained? RadixArk built about 1,200 curated tasks with Eigent AI , chosen from thousands of candidates. Each task targets a specific failure of the base model. Each sandbox attempt allows up to 1.5 hours, 100+ tool calls and 256k+ output tokens. Agent sessions reach up to 1M tokens, per the blog . Training ran on Miles , RadixArk’s open-source RL framework, in fully asynchronous mode. The run used 144 H200 GPUs for 18 days. Of those, 128 handled agent inference and 16 handled training. Total compute was 63,000 GPU-hours. RadixArk reports 37% MFU on its internal backend. An open-source Megatron-based trainer reached 16%. End-to-end throughput was 16.8k tokens/s versus 8.3k, a 2.0x speedup. RadixArk says this cut GPU time by 57%. Sandboxes ran on AgentENV . RadixArk reports about 944,000 sandboxes from mid-September to mid-November. Peak concurrency hit 1,566. Creation success was 99% over 9 weeks. RadixArk puts the cost about 80% below popular cloud sandbox providers. How does DaisyRose-27B perform on benchmarks? All scores are self-reported by RadixArk. DaisyRose scores are the higher of its BF16 and FP8 runs. Benchmark DaisyRose-27B Qwen3.8-27B Change Terminal Bench 4.1 (pass@1) 12.0 5.6 +6.4 Terminal Bench 2.1 75.5 73.0 +2.5 DeepSWE v1.1 46.2 42.2 +4.0 SWE Bench Pro v2 94.7 91.3 +3.4 HLE (text only) 34.3 33.9 +0.4 IFBench 82.4 79.5 +2.9 GPQA Diamond 90.7 89.2 +1.5 Source: RadixArk blog and model card . The largest jump is Terminal Bench 4.1, which more than doubles. Coding gains are steady: +4.0 on DeepSWE v1.1 and +3.4 on SWE Bench Pro v2. Knowledge gains are small, at +0.4 on HLE and +1.5 on GPQA Diamond. Against larger models, results are mixed. MiMo V2.6 Flash (309B total) leads Terminal Bench 4.1 at 16.1. content.entityName: NVIDIA AI Releases Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, a Continuous Diffusion Language Model with 14 checkpoints at 3B/8B

data.title: NVIDIA AI Releases Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, a Continuous Diffusion Language Model with 14 checkpoints at 3B/8B
data.summary: NVIDIA released Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, 14 open 3B and 8B continuous diffusion language model checkpoints. Sigma denoises text in a learned 16-D embedding space, distills to few-step samplers, and decodes up to 4.20x faster than autoregressive decoding. The post NVIDIA AI Releases Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, a Continuous Diffusion Language Model with 14 checkpoints at 3B/8B appeared first on MarkTechPost .
data.content:
NVIDIA has released Nemotron-Labs-Sigma , a collection of 14 open checkpoints at 3B and 8B scale. Nemotron-Labs-Sigma is a continuous diffusion language model family that denoises text in a 16-D embedding space. Most diffusion LLMs, such as LLaDA and Dream, work on discrete tokens. Sigma works in a smooth latent space instead. NVIDIA team states that this makes few-step distillation and trajectory steering practical for text. TL;DR Size: 3B and 8B parameters, 14 checkpoints. Context is 4,096 tokens (8,192 for Sigma-8B-instruct). Runs on: 1 NVIDIA GPU in bfloat16 (Ampere, Lovelace, Hopper, Blackwell). About 120 to 140 tokens/s on 1 H100. No CPU support, no quantized variants listed. Performance: Sigma-8B base averages 71.16 on NVIDIA’s 6-task suite, ahead of NLD-8B (70.22). Best: 91.96 on GSM8K (Sigma-8B-instruct, 256 DDPM steps). Worst: 17.00 on AIME25 (same model and sampler). Bottom line: Best: the 8-step distilled 8B keeps a 70.34 average. Worst: the instruct average (59.14) trails NLD-8B (59.92). What is Nemotron-Labs-Sigma? The research team calls Sigma the first large-scale family of continuous diffusion language models. The collection has 4 variant types at each size: Base: Sigma-3B and Sigma-8B. Instruct: Sigma-3B-instruct and Sigma-8B-instruct. Few-step distilled: distill-3B and distill-8B at NFE 2, 4, 8 and 16 (8 checkpoints). Self-speculative: distill-spec-3B and distill-spec-8B. How does continuous diffusion for language work? Each token maps to a point in a learned 16-D embedding space . Training adds Gaussian noise to these embeddings and teaches the model to remove it. The embedding geometry is learned jointly with the denoiser. Generation runs blockwise. Each denoised block is committed to a KV cache before the next starts. Blocks default to 64 tokens. The backbone is a Ministral-style decoder-only Transformer with grouped-query attention, SwiGLU and rotary embeddings. Training starts from an autoregressive warm start of about 1T tokens. About 0.3T tokens of diffusion training follow. At inference, classifier-free guidance and score temperature matter most. The model card page recommends guidance 3 and temperature 0.3 at 32 DDIM steps. Why does a continuous space matter? Discrete diffusion jumps between token states, so its trajectories are hard to steer. Sigma follows smooth ODE/SDE paths instead. Per the research paper , these degrade gracefully at low step counts and distill efficiently. Embedding-space steering also tunes the quality-diversity trade-off for pass@k sampling. How does Sigma perform on benchmarks? On the research’s 6-task base suite, Sigma-8B with 256 DDPM steps averages 71.16. NLD-8B in diffusion mode scores 70.22, Dream-7B 58.74 and LLaDA-8B 41.78. Qwen3-8B in AR mode scores 68.91. A cheaper 32-step DDIM sampler still gives Sigma-8B a 70.18 average. Coding is the standout. Sigma-8B scores 65.12 on HumanEval versus 62.80 for NLD-8B. MBPP is weaker, at 65.74 versus 67.00. After SFT, Sigma-8B-instruct scores 91.96 on GSM8K, 78.40 on MATH-500 and 82.50 on HumanEval. Hard reasoning stays limited, at 23.33 on AIME24 and 17.00 on AIME25. Its 10-task average of 59.14 sits just below NLD-8B at 59.92. All scores are NVIDIA’s own evaluations. Back

"> How fast are the distilled and speculative checkpoints? Sigma-distill-8B-nfe8 decodes each 32-token block in 8 denoiser calls plus 1 readout. Its card reports a 6-task mean of 70.34, with 88.44 on GSM8K and 65.18 on HumanEval. That is close to the 256-step teacher. NVIDIA’s launch thread frames the gain as 8 tokens per forward on math and 4 on code. The distill-spec checkpoints add self-speculative decoding. A diffusion head drafts a 32-token block, and the model’s own AR head verifies it. Output exactly matches greedy AR decoding. On 1 GB200 with SGLang, the 8B spec model runs 3.46x faster than AR decoding on average. NLD-8B reaches 3.04x on the same setup. Peak speedups reach 4.20x at 8B and 3.18x at 3B. How do you deploy Nemotron-Labs-Sigma? All 14 checkpoints are on Hugging Face under the NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model License. The cards state the models are ready for commercial use. You need a CUDA GPU in bfloat16: Ampere, Lovelace, Hopper or Blackwell. CPU inference is not supported. Loading needs PyTorch 2.4+, Transformers 4.55+ and trust_remote_code . On 1 H100, the base model generates about 120 to 140 tokens/s. The distilled card lists vLLM, SGLang and Docker Model Runner for serving. NVIDIA hosts no API. How does Sigma compare with other 8B diffusion and AR models? Benchmark rows use NVIDIA’s evaluations from the Sigma paper (Table 2 base, Table 5 instruct). Specs come from each model’s own card. content.entityName: Meta FAIR Self-Improving Memory Hits 56.0 on Continual Learning Bench

data.title: Meta FAIR Self-Improving Memory Hits 56.0 on Continual Learning Bench
data.summary: Meta FAIR’s Self-Improving Memory lets Kimi-K2.6 write its own LOAD and OFFLOAD memory prompts, then distills them into its weights. Optimized prompts score 56.0 versus 44.6 for the best hand-written harness on Continual Learning Bench. The post Meta FAIR Self-Improving Memory Hits 56.0 on Continual Learning Bench appeared first on MarkTechPost .
data.content: Meta FAIR has introduced Self-Improving Memory , a method for AI agents that manage their own memory. The model first discovers its own memory instructions. It then trains those skills into its weights. Co-authors include researchers from the University of Washington and Johns Hopkins University. TL;DR Method: The base is Kimi-K2.6 , a 1T-parameter MoE with 32B active and 256K context. Distillation adds a LoRA adapter (rank 64) on attention projections. Runs on: Training hardware is not disclosed. Kimi-K2.6 serving needs a multi-GPU node; Vast.ai recommends 8x H200 . Native INT4 weights exist. Performance: Self-found memory prompts average 56.0 on 3 tasks, versus 44.6 for the best human-written ones. Best: Codebase, 64.3 with optimized prompts, +20.6 over the best hand-written harness. Worst: Spectrum distillation adds only 2.9 points (46.5 vs 43.6 for SFT on generic runs). What is Self-Improving Memory? Self-Improving Memory is a 2-stage method from Meta FAIR that teaches an agent model to manage file-based memory. The agent works through a stream of subtasks. Each subtask starts with an empty context. Only a persistent memory directory, edited with file tools, carries over. Two prompts control that memory. OFFLOAD updates memory after a subtask. LOAD retrieves notes before the next one. Generic versions leave the strategy to the model. A pilot study in the research post found that no single hand-written strategy wins every task. How does harness optimization work? In stage 1, a meta agent rewrites the LOAD and OFFLOAD prompts. The search starts from 4 human-written seeds: Summary, Retrieval, Skill and Hypothesis. Each candidate runs the full task stream 5 times. The top 4 by mean score become parents for revision. For each parent, the meta agent reads trajectories, scores and final memory directories. It then proposes revised prompts. Selection uses a holdout set the meta agent cannot see. The discovered prompts are concrete. One Database prompt says to read GUARDRAILS.md, then SCHEMA.md, before answering. The best Codebase design uses a quickstart file, an indexed fix registry and separate fix files. How does harness distillation move the gains into weights? Stage 2 follows a Discover-Demonstrate-Distill pipeline. The task agent runs train subtasks with the optimized prompts. Every model call is logged. The research team then swaps the optimized prompts back to the generic ones in that history. The swap works because the behavior stays valid under generic instructions. Examples include keeping QUICKSTART.md, REGISTRY.md and SCHEMA.md files, and verifying join keys before aggregation. The model is fine-tuned with LoRA, rank 64, on attention projection layers. The loss covers only assistant tokens, including reasoning and tool calls. Each task gets equal weight. The meta agent and task agent are the same Kimi-K2.6 model. So the model is trained on memory skills it discovered itself. What do the benchmarks show? The tests use 3 Continual Learning Bench tasks: Database (SQL), Codebase (repo fixes) and Spectrum (radio scans). Test subtasks follow a designed phase shift. So results measure generalization to new instances of the same tasks. Test score Database Codebase Spectrum Average No memory 7.5 31.8 21.9 20.4 Compaction 39.8 36.9 34.6 37.1 Generic harness 32.3 33.5 42.5 36.1 Best human-written 47.9 43.7 42.1 44.6 Optimized harness 53.8 64.3 49.9 56.0 SFT on generic trajectories 31.6 37.5 43.6 37.6 SFT on optimized trajectories (generic prompts) 37.7 45.1 46.5 43.1 Source: Figures 4 and 5, Self-Improving Memory blog . Kimi-K2.6 for all rows. Optimized harnesses beat the best hand-written seed on all 3 tasks. Codebase gained the most, at 20.6 points. Search was noisy: 37 of 44 generated revisions failed to beat the previous best. Database and Spectrum peaked in the first generation. Codebase kept improving through generation 4. After distillation, every model runs the generic harness. The distilled model averages 43.1 across 10 matched seeds. SFT on generic trajectories reaches 37.6. That is a 5.5-point gain, or 14.6%. && How does it compare with ALMA, MemEvolve and Harness-Zero? Several recent methods search over agent memory or harnesses. Self-Improving Memory searches memory prompts, then distills them into weights. Benchmarks differ, so headline numbers are not directly comparable. Feature Self-Improving Memory ALMA MemEvolve Harness-Zero Org FAIR at Meta, UW, JHU Xiong, Hu, Clune OPPO AI Agent Team, LV-NUS Peking University, Google, HKUST What is searched LOAD/OFFLOAD memory prompts Memory designs as Python code Memory architecture and contents Full agent harness Trains weights Yes, LoRA rank 64 No No Yes, LoRA SFT Models Kimi-K2.6 (agent and meta agent) GPT-5 meta agent, GPT-5-nano/mini task agent GPT-5-mini (plus DeepSeek V3.2, Kimi K2) Qwen3.5-9B student Benchmarks Continual Learning Bench (3 tasks) ALFWorld, TextWorld, Baba Is AI, MiniHack GAIA, WebWalkerQA, xBench-DeepSearch, TaskCraft SpreadsheetBench Verified, AppWorld, USPTO Retrosynthesis Headline result 56.0 vs 44.6 best human harness; 43.1 distilled 53.9% vs 41.1% no memory (GPT-5-mini) Up to 17.06% gains 23.3% to 44.3% with harness removed Code Not released GitHub GitHub GitHub Harness-Zero is the closest match, but it uses a separate agent to correct the student. Self-Improving Memory skips that step. Key Takeaways Kimi-K2.6 writes memory prompts that beat human ones: 56.0 vs 44.6. Codebase sees the biggest jump: 64.3, up 20.6 points. Distillation keeps part of the gain: 43.1 vs 37.6 with generic prompts. 37 of 44 meta-agent revisions failed, so evaluation and selection matter. content.entityName: 13 Best Agent Gateways in 2026 for MCP, A2A and LLM Traffic: Kong, Bifrost, AgentCore, Arcade

data.title: 13 Best Agent Gateways in 2026 for MCP, A2A and LLM Traffic: Kong, Bifrost, AgentCore, Arcade
data.summary: We ranked the 13 best agent gateways of 2026 by how they govern model, MCP tool and agent-to-agent traffic, with verified pricing, deployment options and the trade-offs each vendor's marketing leaves out. The post 13 Best Agent Gateways in 2026 for MCP, A2A and LLM Traffic: Kong, Bifrost, AgentCore, Arcade appeared first on MarkTechPost .
data.content: Agents no longer just call a model. They call tools over MCP, delegate to other agents over A2A, and act inside business systems. The best agent gateways sit on that path and decide who can do what. This list compares 13 of them on traffic coverage, identity, deployment and price. What is an agent gateway? An agent gateway is a control point that authenticates agents, filters the tools they see, and logs every call. A plain LLM gateway only routes model requests. An agent gateway adds MCP tool governance, agent identity and, increasingly, A2A traffic control. Our ranking below is editorial and weighs 5 criteria: traffic coverage, identity and authorization, deployment options, maturity, and price transparency. How the 13 best agent gateways rank 1. Kong AI Gateway Kong governs LLM, MCP and A2A traffic from 1 control plane. Version 2.0 moved AI features into first-class Providers, Models, MCP Servers and Agents entities . Best for: teams already running Kong for API management. Watch out: the 2.x architecture needs a Konnect control plane. Arcade notes the MCP OAuth2 plugin is still Tech Preview. 2. Bifrost (Maxim AI) Bifrost is an Apache 2.0 Go gateway covering models, MCP tools and A2A agents in 1 deployment. Maxim reports 10,000+ models across 25+ providers. Its benchmark claims 11 µs mean overhead at 5,000 RPS . Best for: self-hosted, in-VPC or air-gapped teams that want all 3 traffic types. Watch out: SSO, SCIM and token exchange are Enterprise-only. An independent review notes the 11 µs figure excludes HTTP handling and JSON marshalling. 3. Gravitee AI Gateway Gravitee runs an LLM Proxy, MCP Proxy and A2A Proxy on 1 runtime. All 3 share 1 authentication, policy and OpenTelemetry chain. The A2A Proxy supports RFC 8693 token exchange and skill-level authorization. Best for: enterprises that want agent identity modeled alongside existing APIs. Watch out: Maxim lists Agent Management from $2,500 per month. The A2A Proxy needs Enterprise Edition. 4. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway AgentCore Gateway gives agents 1 managed endpoint for tools, models and other agents . It adds semantic tool search, Cedar policies and on-behalf-of token exchange. Pricing starts at $0.005 per 1,000 invocations . Best for: AWS-native teams using IAM, CloudWatch and Bedrock Guardrails. Watch out: AWS-only. A2A is HTTP passthrough, per Maxim . Search calls cost $0.025 per 1,000 , 5x the invoke rate. 5. Arcade.dev Arcade is an actions runtime, not a model router. Per Arcade , it checks the overlap of user and agent permissions on every action. Credentials never reach the LLM. It lists 8,000+ agent-optimized tools. Best for: agents that write to Salesforce, Gmail or Slack on a user’s behalf. Watch out: no model routing, so pair it with an LLM gateway. Pricing is $25 per month plus $0.10 per auth event and $0.01 per tool call. 6. Prisma AIRS AI Gateway (formerly Portkey) Palo Alto Networks completed its Portkey acquisition in May 2026. The gateway reached GA inside Prisma AIRS in July 2026. Palo Alto describes it as a unified LLM, MCP and A2A gateway with 1 enforcement point. It runs in SaaS and hybrid models . Best for: security teams that want runtime inspection on every prompt. Watch out: pricing is not public. Arcade advises verifying delegated auth and audit depth for agent actions. 7. Azure API Management Microsoft’s AI gateway extends API Management to model APIs, MCP servers and A2A agent APIs. It can expose REST APIs as MCP servers and front existing MCP servers. Best for: Microsoft-centric API teams. Watch out: A2A support is preview, JSON-RPC only, and limited to v2 tiers. 8. Google Cloud Agent Gateway Agent Gateway is the network entry and exit point for Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It assigns each agent a SPIFFE ID and can apply Model Armor to prompts and responses. Maxim lists up to 5,000 governed resources per gateway. Best for: teams building on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Watch out: Maxim reports cross-cloud support as “coming soon.” Model routing and fallback are not documented. 9. IBM ContextForge ContextForge is an Apache 2.0 registry and proxy that federates MCP, REST, gRPC and A2A. It exposes agents as MCP tools and, per Maxim , deploys via Helm. Best for: free, MCP-first, self-hosted Kubernetes setups. Watch out: no published commercial support. IBM recommends upgrading to v1.1.1 after security bulletins covering v1.0.0 to v1.1.0. 10. Agent Router (formerly Envoy AI Gateway) Envoy AI Gateway became Agent Router and joined the Agentic AI Foundation in September 2026. It offers an OpenAI-compatible API plus an MCP gateway on Envoy. Best for: Kubernetes teams already on Envoy Gateway. Watch out: A2A is preview and JSON-RPC only. Maxim notes no built-in guardrails. 11. Composio Composio is an MCP gateway and SaaS integration layer with managed OAuth and per-user connected accounts. Arcade lists a free tier of 100,000 tool calls per month and Pro from $29. Best for: fast access to a large prebuilt SaaS catalog. Watch out: Arcade notes sessions are discoverable by default unless allowlisted. 12. TrueFoundry TrueFoundry combines an LLM Gateway and centralized MCP access with training and deployment tooling. Pro costs $25 per user per month , with 20,000 requests and tool calls per user. Best for: ML teams that want gateway and MLOps in 1 platform. Watch out: the client-credentials MCP flow uses a shared identity, not the user’s, Arcade notes . 13. Obot Obot is an open-source platform bundling an MCP Gateway, LLM Gateway and device monitoring. It supports per-user auth, OAuth token exchange and audit logs. Best for: IT teams rolling out MCP servers to employees. Watch out: self-hosting alone does not settle downstream authorization, Arcade notes . Agent gateway comparison table Gateway LLM MCP A2A Open source Deployment Entry price Kong AI Gateway Yes Yes Yes Gateway core only Hybrid (Konnect CP) Usage-based Bifrost Yes Yes Yes Yes (Apache 2.0) Self-hosted, VPC, air-gapped Free OSS Gravitee Yes Yes Yes (Enterprise) Not disclosed Self-hosted, hybrid, SaaS $2,500/mo AgentCore Gateway Yes Yes Passthrough No AWS managed $0.005 / 1K calls Arcade.dev No Yes Not documented Framework only Cloud, VPC, air-gapped Free; $25/mo Prisma AIRS AI Gateway Yes Yes Yes No SaaS, hybrid Not disclosed Azure API Management Yes Yes Preview No Azure, self-hosted gateway Not disclosed Google Agent Gateway Not documented Yes Yes No Google Cloud Agent Compute usage IBM ContextForge Yes Yes Via MCP / passthrough Yes (Apache 2.0) Self-hosted (Helm) Free Agent Router Yes Yes Preview Yes (Apache 2.0) Self-hosted (Kubernetes) Free Composio No Yes Not documented Not disclosed Cloud, enterprise self-host Free; $29/mo TrueFoundry Yes Yes Not documented No Cloud, on-prem Free; $25/user/mo Obot Yes Yes Not documented Yes Self-hosted, Obot Cloud Free (Community) & How to choose an agent gateway Start with traffic. If agents only call models, an LLM gateway is enough. If they call tools, you need MCP governance. If they delegate to other agents, check A2A support carefully. Then check identity. Ask whether user and agent permissions are enforced separately at execution time. Finally, check where it must run: single cloud, your VPC, or air-gapped. Key Takeaways Only Kong, Bifrost, Gravitee and Prisma AIRS govern LLM, MCP and A2A natively. A2A support is the weakest link: preview, passthrough or JSON-RPC only elsewhere. Cloud gateways (AWS, Azure, Google) win on integration but lock you in. Arcade solves a different problem: governed actions, not model routing. Most identity features (SSO, token exchange) sit behind enterprise licenses. content.entityName: Perplexity Launches Orchestrator API for Failover and Model Routing

data.title: Perplexity Launches Orchestrator API for Failover and Model Routing
data.summary: Perplexity’s Orchestrator API serves OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI and open-weight models through 1 endpoint, with same-model provider failover, unified billing and a preview perplexity/auto router that sends each request to a described route. The post Perplexity Launches Orchestrator API for Failover and Model Routing appeared first on MarkTechPost .
data.content: Perplexity has launched the Perplexity Orchestrator API , a single endpoint for frontier and open-weight models. It picks a serving provider by availability, capacity and latency , and bills everything through 1 account. Developers get fewer integrations and 1 invoice. What is the Perplexity Orchestrator API? The Perplexity Orchestrator API is a hosted inference gateway that serves many models behind 1 base URL. It covers frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI . It also serves open-weight models such as GLM, Kimi and DeepSeek, hosted by Perplexity or inference partners. It accepts OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages requests. Most teams only change the API key and base URL. The OpenAI base URL is https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator/v1 . Anthropic SDK users point at https://api.perplexity.ai/orchestrator , without /v1 . Perplexity runs the same layer internally, across 85+ models and more than a dozen providers. How does provider failover work? Failover keeps the model fixed and swaps the deployment. A Claude request that fails on Anthropic can be served by AWS Bedrock instead. The reliability docs set these rules: Triggers are provider errors, rate limits and timeouts. Each attempt has a time-to-first-token limit and a total-duration limit. The values are not published. Invalid or over-context requests return HTTP 400 and are not retried. If every deployment fails, the API returns HTTP 429 with Retry-After . Requests that fail before producing output are not billed. You cannot pick a deployment yourself. What do the reliability and speed numbers show? Perplexity measured production traffic from October 4 to November 2, 2026. Claude and GPT requests through Perplexity succeeded more often than requests to any single provider measured. Daily success rates also varied less during provider incidents. The post gives no percentage success rates. Speed varied by provider too. For Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic was fastest on 15 of 30 days, AWS Bedrock on 15. Azure’s median output speed for GPT-5.6 Sol was 27% higher than OpenAI’s. Speed-aware routing is still in progress. How does automatic routing with perplexity/auto work? Routing is in preview. You set model to perplexity/auto and pass a routing object. It holds a default_model and 1 to 5 routes , each with a name, description and model. A decision model reads the conversation and route descriptions. It never sees route names or model IDs. If nothing matches, or the decision model fails or times out, the default model answers. So do media inputs. Response headers report the result: x-perplexity-autoroute-outcome , -route and -confidence . The default policy sends traffic to GPT-6.1 Sol, with simple requests going to GPT-6 Luna. Perplexity also lists built-in Lower cost, Balanced and Higher quality profiles, plus an Auto effort preview. && Can routing work around refusals? Perplexity tested this on a 63-task subset of Terminal-Bench 4.1 , run in Claude Code. Anthropic documents that Claude Fable 5.2 safeguards can block benign security and life sciences work. Claude Fable 5.2 alone: 38/63 tasks. Fable plus routes to GPT-6.1 Sol: 41/63. Fable plus routes to GPT-6 Astra: 41/63. The routes covered security , biology and after_refusal requests. That is +3 tasks, at a higher estimated cost per task. Perplexity calls it an adjusted comparison; results vary by workload. How is Orchestrator priced? Each request is billed at the answering model’s published per-token rate. Failover to another provider does not change the rate. Perplexity says there is no additional platform fee on top of credits . For example, perplexity/glm-5.3 lists $1.4 input, $4.4 output and $0.26 cache read per 1M tokens . Usage draws from prepaid Perplexity API credits, also purchasable through AWS Marketplace. Access is tiered by cumulative credit purchases : Tier 0: Google, xAI and open-weight models. Tier 1 ($50): OpenAI and most Anthropic models. Tier 2 ($250): Claude Opus 5, Opus 5.5 and the Fable models. How does it compare with OpenRouter and Vercel AI Gateway? Feature Perplexity Orchestrator OpenRouter Vercel AI Gateway Model catalog Frontier (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI) plus open-weight GLM, Kimi, DeepSeek; count not disclosed ( blog ) 400+ models, 70+ providers ( source ) 400+ models ( source ) API formats Chat Completions, Responses, Anthropic Messages ( docs ) Chat Completions, Responses, Anthropic Messages ( docs ) Chat Completions, Responses, Anthropic Messages ( docs ) Platform fee No additional platform fee on credits ( blog ) 5.5% on credit purchases (Standard), 8% (Business) ( pricing ) No platform fee, no token markup ( pricing ) Token pricing Answering model’s published rate ( FAQ ) Provider price passed through ( FAQ ) Provider list price ( docs ) Same-model provider failover Yes, automatic ( docs ) Yes, automatic fallback ( source ) Yes, automatic ( changelog ) Prompt-based auto router perplexity/auto , preview, 1 to 5 routes ( docs ) openrouter/auto , no router fee ( docs ) Not disclosed Bring your own key Not supported ( FAQ ) Supported, 5% fee above allowance ( FAQ ) Supported, no markup ( docs ) Key Takeaways 1 endpoint for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI and open-weight models. Same-model failover across providers, billed at the same rate. perplexity/auto routes by plain-language descriptions, in preview. Refusal routing: 38/63 to 41/63 on Terminal-Bench 4.1, self-reported. content.entityName: Not If, But How: Responding to Security Incidents in the Age of AI Attackers

data.title: Not If, But How: Responding to Security Incidents in the Age of AI Attackers
data.summary: AI-powered attackers are driving more frequent attacks on AI infrastructure. This guide reviews 6 months of incidents, sets out a 4-pillar incident response playbook, and shows it in practice through Fireworks AI and Klue. The post Not If, But How: Responding to Security Incidents in the Age of AI Attackers appeared first on MarkTechPost .
data.content: Attackers now have powerful AI on their side. AI agents can scan, plan and run intrusions at machine speed, and they improve every month. The result is more attacks, more often and at global scale. In that environment, more companies will face a security incident at some point. What separates them is how they respond. Machine-speed threats call for a modern playbook with 4 pillars. Detect and contain automatically. Communicate fast and securely. Eradicate thoroughly. Keep shrinking the blast radius. This article shows the trend through 6 months of incidents. It then looks at a few companies, with Fireworks AI as a model of mature, structurally sound response. TL;DR The trend: AI-powered attackers are driving more frequent attacks at global scale. The evidence: Several AI platforms disclosed security incidents between May and November 2026. Pillar 1: Detect and contain automatically. Human-speed shutdowns are too slow. Pillar 2: Communicate fast and securely, over out-of-band channels. Pillar 3: Eradicate thoroughly, with outside forensic experts. Pillar 4: Keep shrinking the blast radius. Data that is never stored cannot be stolen. Case studies: Fireworks AI and Klue show these pillars in practice. Why are attacks becoming more frequent? AI has changed the economics of attacking. Tasks that took skilled people days can now be delegated to agents. In November, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said AI misuse had reached a “critical inflection point” . They report that attackers use AI to shorten timelines and run multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. CrowdStrike reported that 1 group used AI agents against more than 200 organizations in 11 days . Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 found attacks moving about 4 times faster than a year earlier. The shift started earlier. In 2025, Anthropic disrupted a campaign where AI did 80 to 90% of tactical work with little human input. The tools keep improving, so the pace will keep rising. AI infrastructure is an especially attractive target, because AI access itself has value. The last 6 months show what that looks like. What was disclosed in the last 6 months? Incidents appeared across every layer of the AI stack. Together they show how broad the activity has become. May: package registries. On May 10 and 11, the “Mini Shai-Hulud” campaign altered about 170 npm packages and some PyPI libraries . Affected projects included AI SDKs from Mistral AI and Guardrails AI. The NHS cyber alert lists the specific versions to avoid. June: SaaS integrations. Klue, a market intelligence platform, disclosed misuse of OAuth tokens it held for customers. See case study 2. August: self-hosted AI gateways. Microsoft described intrusions into exposed, unpatched LiteLLM, RAGFlow and Kestra deployments. Fixed versions exist for all 3 tools . CISA had listed the LiteLLM flaw as known exploited on June 8. September: evaluation environments. Anthropic’s September threat report described attempts to obtain AI keys through software vendors. The Cloud Security Alliance summarized it . In 1 case, instructions were injected into a vendor’s automated evaluation sandbox. October and early November: developer platforms. At least 9 AI developer and hosting platforms disclosed incidents involving stored customer secrets in October. Wiz’s tracker later listed further disclosures, for 16 platforms in total. A tampered LiteLLM release, version 1.107.0, was also identified , and users were told to roll back. November: shared web vendors. On November 16, an attacker abused a flaw in Optimizely’s account signup flow to inject code into customer projects, reaching 178 organizations’ websites, according to Report URI, including HSBC, Salesforce, the BBC and Ledger. The code swapped crypto wallet addresses and skimmed payment forms; Optimizely removed the payload and fixed the flaw. Hudson Rock traced similar code through three other web services, beginning November 13. It is the same concentration pattern, one layer below the AI stack. Date (2026) Platform What was affected Entry point, as reported May 10 to 11 npm and PyPI packages, incl. Mistral AI and Guardrails AI SDKs Developer and CI credentials on installing hosts Poisoned package releases June 11 to 12 Klue Customer Salesforce and Gong data Legacy credential, then stored OAuth tokens August LiteLLM, RAGFlow, Kestra deployments Model provider keys, backend access Exposed, unpatched gateways October 6 Fireworks AI Environment variables in evaluation jobs, limited accounts Misused internal credentials October 14 to 15 Zeabur 3,218,965 environment variable records, 321,810 accounts Long-lived admin tokens, exposed admin interface October 15 Lightning AI Credentials; Studio taken offline Credential access October 16 to 17 OpenCode OpenAI, Anthropic and Google keys of about 1.4% of Console users Legacy system October 20 to 21 Railway Encrypted environment variables, some decrypted Privilege escalation in build infrastructure October 21 LiteLLM 1.107.0 Cloud credentials and LLM keys on installing hosts Release pipeline compromise October 23 Warp Agent decision logs and telemetry, about 1% of users Third-party vendor dependency October 23 to 24 Fireworks AI Billing data; for some customers, datasets and incomplete model weights Incident at a third-party cloud provider October 29 Cursor Altered extension copy in its marketplace cache, up to 5,000 users Credential from exposed internal data October 30 Northflank Customers told to assume environment variables were decrypted Not disclosed November 8 NEAR AI Inference server; 2 API keys exposed in logs Remote code execution flaw in SGLang Selected incidents: Dates follow the linked sources, which sometimes differ by a day. Several October entries rely on compilations by Wiz and Helix rather than primary vendor disclosures. What do these incidents have in common? There was no single vulnerability. According to the Cloud Security Alliance, entry points varied . The common target was stored environment variables, often holding AI provider API keys. AI keys carry real value, which explains the interest. CSA, citing Anthropic, notes that a key can be resold, used for compute or used as cover . Wiz estimated that misuse of 2 keys from these incidents exceeded $100,000 at list price . That is why spending caps matter. Concentration is the other shared factor. A platform that stores secrets for many customers naturally draws attention. CSA describes this as the platform-chain pattern . What does a modern incident response playbook look like? No company can promise it will never be breached. Every company can control how it responds. Against attackers that move at machine speed, that response rests on 4 pillars. 1. Detect and contain automatically: A human-speed shutdown is no longer enough. An AI-driven intruder can move between systems in minutes. Mature teams wire detection directly to containment. That means kill-switches, automatic token revocation and host isolation. Wiz recommends alerting on bulk secret reads , the clearest signal in this year’s incidents. The best setups act on that signal automatically. 2. Communicate fast, and securely: Speed still matters most for revocation. Customers need to rotate keys, and upstream providers need to revoke access at the source. CSA notes that deleting a key from a platform does not revoke it . Mature teams also choose the channel with care. A Five Eyes joint advisory warns against communicating over the network under investigation . It advises out-of-band communication instead. CISA’s playbooks likewise call for out-of-band communications infrastructure as part of preparation. That keeps an attacker who is still watching from learning the response plan. 3. Eradicate thoroughly: Closing the hole that was used is only the first step. Top teams assume the attacker planted backdoors and hunt for them. They bring in independent forensic experts, such as Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 or Mandiant. The same advisory recommends third-party incident response support . It also warns against fixing symptoms instead of the root cause. 4. Keep improving by shrinking the blast radius: Attackers improve every month, so security is never finished. The strongest proactive defense limits what any future attacker can reach. Zero Trust access means no credential is trusted by default. Ephemeral architecture means sensitive data is not kept at all. If data isn’t stored, it can’t be stolen. Some companies already apply these pillars. The 2 case studies below show how: Case study 1: How did Fireworks AI respond? Fireworks AI is an inference and training platform. It disclosed an incident in October, 2026, during a busy month for the industry. Its response is a strong example of mature, structurally sound incident response across the 4 pillars. Pillar 1: detect and contain Fireworks identified unauthorized use of internal credentials on October 6 . A second event began on October 24, through a third-party cloud provider that hosted its R&D machines. Fireworks detected that activity and closed it on the same day it began. That is the kind of operational agility machine-speed threats demand. Pillar 2: communicate fast Fireworks began notifying affected customers on October 7 , about 1 day after detection . It published a public bulletin on October 9 and has updated it as findings came in. It also notified law enforcement. The bulletin lists affected resource metadata and billing information. For certain customers, it also lists datasets, incomplete model weights and secrets. Pillar 3: eradicate thoroughly Fireworks engaged Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for forensic analysis. Bringing in an independent, top-tier team is a mature decision. It means the investigation looks beyond the first entry point, for anything an attacker may have left behind. Fireworks also completed rotation of employee API keys by October 9 . Pillar 4: a smaller blast radius by design Fireworks’ most important protection was already in place. It says it detected no impact to its Inference, Training SDK and Nexus products. All 3 run with zero data retention by default, so prompts and outputs are not stored at rest. That architecture kept the core products out of the reported impact. Fireworks has since gone further. It paused its Batch API , and its documentation says stored Batch inputs and outputs will be permanently deleted. Enterprise customers can also enforce an account-wide ZDR policy . The philosophy behind it: On November 13, 2026, Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao posted on X to explain the company’s data retention policy. She described 2 standard API designs: Customer-managed retention (upload, use, delete). A user uploads a dataset, runs jobs on it, then deletes it. Batch APIs are the typical example. The platform keeps the data until told to delete it, because it cannot know when the user is finished. Cleanup is the user’s job. Fireworks says it does not retain data after deletion. Ephemeral processing (send, compute, return). The platform processes a request and returns the result without keeping the content. This is zero data retention. Fireworks applies it to its inference APIs, its Training SDK, including serverless training, and Nexus. Prompts and generations are not persisted at rest. She compared it to saving a spreadsheet in a cloud drive versus passing its numbers to a calculator. In both designs, customers control their data. Her conclusion is that ephemeral processing is preferable whenever the workflow allows it. It leaves no forgotten datasets or missed deletion calls, and every retained copy is something to protect. In our view, this is the gold standard for proactive defense, and the October events bear it out. Some customers, including Cursor, Uber and Notion, have published their own notices. Investigations are ongoing. The lesson: same-day containment, fast notice and independent forensics limit an incident’s duration. Ephemeral architecture limits what can be reached at all. Case study 2: How did Klue respond? Klue is a market intelligence platform that connects to customer CRM and sales tools. Its June incident shows the same habits in a different part of the stack. What happened. On June 11 and 12, an attacker used a compromised legacy credential tied to Klue’s integration service. With it, they obtained OAuth tokens Klue held for customers. Those tokens were used to read data from some connected Salesforce and Gong environments. Pillars 1 and 2: detect and communicate. Klue identified the activity on June 12 and notified customers the same day . Same-day notice let customers start reviewing their own connected systems at once. Pillars 1 and 3: contain and eradicate. Klue revoked affected credentials and disabled 9 integrations, including Salesforce, HubSpot, Gong and Slack. Salesforce disabled the Klue integration on June 17 . The lesson: every stored token is standing access. Retiring old credentials and long-lived tokens is pillar 4 in practice for integration platforms. What do the two case studies have in common? Both companies held something on behalf of customers: datasets and secrets at Fireworks, OAuth tokens at Klue. Both detected the activity and notified customers within about a day. Both cut off access at the source. Fireworks went further on pillars 3 and 4, with independent forensics and an architecture that stores less by default. Who is responsible when an AI platform has an incident? Usually more than 1 party. Most of these events ran through a chain of companies, and each link plays a role. Upstream suppliers: Cloud providers, package registries and build tools sit beneath every platform. Fireworks’ second event began at a third-party cloud provider . The May package campaign and the LiteLLM release began in build and publishing pipelines . The platform or provider: A platform that holds customer secrets is responsible for protecting them. CSA calls platform operators a main point of control . The vendor building on the platform: Companies that integrate an AI API decide what they send, store and share. When they use upload-based features, deleting data they no longer need is part of their job. In Cursor’s case, the key opened a bucket Cursor used to share data with Fireworks . Some traces in it held unredacted credentials, which reached Cursor’s own tools. Cursor has since added secret scanning and rotated its credentials. The end customer: Keys stay valid until the issuing provider revokes them. CSA suggests treating each long-lived key as exposed if a platform holding it reports an incident . Good choices at any link can contain an incident. That is why the guidance below is split by role. What do the incidents show about stored data? A useful lesson comes from what was not affected. Cursor reports that prompts and code from Privacy Mode users were not affected . That data was never kept, so there was nothing to copy. The pattern holds across the timeline. Incidents involved stored items: environment variables, OAuth tokens, datasets, logs and traces. Live requests processed in memory were not among the reported impacts. This is the practical case for ephemeral processing. Fewer stored copies mean fewer things to protect, track and delete. What should each party do next? The guidance below draws on CSA, Wiz and government incident response advice. AI providers and platforms Deploy automated containment triggers for bulk secret reads. Revoke tokens and isolate workloads without waiting for a human. Retire non-expiring admin tokens, and keep admin interfaces off the public internet. Separate internal workloads from customer workloads. Set up out-of-band communication channels before an incident, and use them during it. Notify customers, partners, upstream providers and law enforcement quickly. Measure notice time in hours. Retain an independent forensic firm in advance, so eradication can start on day 1. Adopt ephemeral architecture and zero data retention wherever workflows allow. Offer spending caps and short-lived credentials by default. Vendors building on AI APIs Prefer ephemeral, zero data retention endpoints. As Lin Qiao puts it, use them whenever the workflow allows . When you do upload data, own the delete step. Set expiry dates on shared buckets and datasets, and delete them when the job ends. Scan prompts, traces and datasets for secrets before they leave your systems. Issue 1 key per platform and per application, so revocation stays narrow. Ask suppliers how fast they detect, contain and notify, and whether they use outside forensics. Every team holding AI keys Rotate at the issuing provider. Deleting a key from a platform does not revoke it . Set spending and rate caps that match expected use. Review usage and billing logs after any supplier notice. Key Takeaways AI-powered attackers are making attacks faster, more frequent and more global. Modern response rests on 4 pillars: contain automatically, communicate securely, eradicate thoroughly, shrink the blast radius. Zero data retention kept companies like Fireworks’ core products out of the reported impact. If data isn’t stored, it can’t be stolen. content.entityName: Google DeepMind Releases Gemini 4 Neon: 1M Context, #1 on AA Coding Agent Index

data.title: Google DeepMind Releases Gemini 4 Neon: 1M Context, #1 on AA Coding Agent Index
data.summary: Google released Gemini 4 Neon, a 1M-context Gemini 4 model priced at $3/$15 per million tokens. It scores 61 on the AA Intelligence Index and ranks #1 on AA’s Coding Agent Index. The post Google DeepMind Releases Gemini 4 Neon: 1M Context, #1 on AA Coding Agent Index appeared first on MarkTechPost .
data.content: Google DeepMind just released Gemini 4 Neon . Gemini 4 Neon is a reasoning model that sits between Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen. It targets coding agents, knowledge work and science workflows. The developer pitch is near-frontier scores at a lower cost per task. Pricing is $3 per 1M input tokens and $15 per 1M output tokens. TL;DR Size: 1M-token unified context, 64K default output, up to 1M via background long decode. Runs on: Google-hosted only. Closed weights, so no local GPU, quantized or edge builds. Performance: 61 on the AA Intelligence Index, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (59) and GPT-6.2 Sol (57). Best: 95.2% on GraphWalks (256K to 1M context), vs 80.1% for GPT-6.2 Sol. Worst: 46.2% on FrontierCode 2.0, behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 47.3%. Bottom line: Best: leads long-context and agentic coding at $3/$15. Worst: closed, self-reported, pricier per token than GPT-6.2 Sol. What is Gemini 4 Neon? Neon is the middle model in the Gemini 4 family. Carbon handles the hardest long-horizon projects. Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution. Neon balances depth and efficiency between the two. As per the model card , Neon is adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon. Google does not disclose parameter count or architecture. Inputs cover text, images, audio and video. The knowledge cutoff is March 2026. How does Neon work inside agent workflows? Neon exposes multiple thinking levels. High is the default. xhigh is reserved for the hardest engineering, analytical and science workloads. For long agent runs, Neon supports context compaction and makes fewer redundant file reads. In Google Antigravity , Neon can act as an orchestrator. It directs parallel Gemini 4 Hydrogen subagents on smaller subtasks. How does Gemini 4 Neon perform on benchmarks? Google compares Neon against Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol. All scores below are reported by Google, not independently reproduced. Coding: #1 on the AA Coding Agent Index at 58.6. SWE-sweep with provider harness hits 39.0%, vs 10.1% for Opus 5.5. Knowledge work: 56.3% on Zapier AutomationBench , vs 42.5% for Opus 5.5. 75.8% on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 . Science and reasoning: 84.0% on RiemannBench , 70.5% on Terminal-Bench-Science and 71.3% on HLE-Diamond . Long context: 95.2% on GraphWalks, vs 66.8% for Opus 5.5. Cyber: 90.5% on SEC-bench Pro , 70.7% on CWE-Bench v2 and 51.3% on WebExploitBench v1.2. Neon does not win every row. Opus 5.5 leads Terminal-bench 4.1 (65.8% vs 65.2%) and FrontierCode 2.0 (47.3% vs 46.2%). GPT-6.2 Sol leads Chartography (75.1% vs 73.5%). On the Vals Index , Neon scores 70.9% and ranks #2. On the Agent Arena index it also ranks #2, with a score of 1336. &&& What does Gemini 4 Neon cost? Neon lists at $3 input, $0.15 cached input and $15 output per 1M tokens. Google says Neon at high thinking costs 32% less per task than Carbon. It also claims 50% to 80% lower cost per task vs rivals on Vals Index and Agent Arena. At xhigh, Google cites 36%+ lower cost than rivals at their highest settings. Those are per-task claims, not per-token prices. GPT-6.2 Sol lists at $2/$10. Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $4/$20. Gemini 4 Carbon is $2/$10 until November 30, then $4/$20. Where can developers use Gemini 4 Neon? Gemini API paid tier, via Google AI Studio and Android Studio Gemini for business , via API and the model dropdown Google Antigravity, for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers The Gemini app , for Pro and Ultra subscribers What do the safety numbers show? Neon runs on the Gemini 4 safety and security stack . Google reports a 0.09% misaligned action rate on its agentic safety suite. It passes 99.2% of the agent honesty evaluation. It shows a 0.0% attack success rate on Gray Swan’s prompt injection benchmark at the highest thinking level. Its 2.45% shortcut rate on a coding cheating test is the lowest of any Gemini 4 model. Gemini 4 Neon vs closest competitors Feature Gemini 4 Neon Gemini 4 Carbon Claude Opus 5.5 GPT-6.2 Sol Developer Google DeepMind Google DeepMind Anthropic OpenAI Parameters Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Weights Closed Closed Closed Closed Context window 1M Not disclosed in launch post 1M 1M Max output 64K default, 1M background Not disclosed 128K Not disclosed Input / output per 1M $3 / $15 $2 / $10 to Nov 30, then $4 / $20 $4 / $20 $2 / $10 AA Intelligence Index 61 Not disclosed 59 57 Vals Index v2.2* 70.9% Not disclosed 70.1% 66.1% Terminal-bench 4.1* 65.2% Not disclosed 65.8% 61.5% SWE-sweep (provider harness)* 39.0% Not disclosed 10.1% 8.3% GraphWalks 256K to 1M* 95.2% Not disclosed 66.8% 80.1% *Scores from Google’s launch comparison table , self-reported. AA scores for Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol match Artificial Analysis . Key Takeaways Neon sits between Carbon and Hydrogen, priced at $3/$15 per 1M tokens. Scores 61 on AA Intelligence Index, #1 on AA Coding Agent Index. Biggest lead: 95.2% on GraphWalks long-context recall. Trails Opus 5.5 on Terminal-bench 4.1 and FrontierCode 2.0.
