content.entityName: Nutrient Data Extraction API: JSON Matching Your Schema With Per-Field Citations and Confidence

data.title: Nutrient Data Extraction API: JSON Matching Your Schema With Per-Field Citations and Confidence
data.summary: Nutrient Data Extraction API parses PDFs, scans and Office files into JSON matching your schema. Fields carry page, region and match-label citations, and Studio lets teams test before writing code. The post Nutrient Data Extraction API: JSON Matching Your Schema With Per-Field Citations and Confidence appeared first on MarkTechPost .
data.content: An LLM presents you a wrong value extracted from a document as fact. That error is costly, especially when basing decisions on it. The Nutrient Data Extraction API targets that problem. It parses PDFs, scans, images and Office files into spatial JSON or Markdown. Extract maps fields from a document onto your JSON schema, and split, classify and form endpoints provide useful primitives for your document pipelines. Each extracted value is anchored to a page via a bounding box, a match label and a confidence score. Nutrient (formerly PSPDFKit) runs the same engine behind an MCP server , agent skill, Mac app and SDK . TL;DR Size: A hosted API with 4 parse modes plus auto routing. Runs on: Nutrient cloud, your own servers via SDK, or an Apple silicon Mac. Where to try it: Studio , a browser workspace to configure and test parsing, extraction,classification, splitting, and form filling. Performance: 86.2 overall on Nutrient’s WholeDoc Bench , top of 19 settings (live API, Agentic). Best: 86.2 at 1.8¢ per page, versus 67.1 at 17.8¢ for the best frontier-model setting. How do you test it in Studio before writing code? Studio is Nutrient’s browser workspace for configuring and testing the API before integrating it in your application. It enables you to test parsing, extraction, classification , splitting, and form filling on your own files. A typical loop: Upload a sample document and set the parameters you plan to send. Draft a schema in the UI, or generate one based on your own documents. Run it on a fresh document, then inspect values and citations. Save the setup as a versioned preset. The API calls it a processor , with a proc_ ID. Score preset versions against up to 25 reviewed documents in an evaluation set. Processors saved in Studio can then be called from the API by ID. Which mode should you pick? Auto routes each page to structure , understand or agentic . If the mode is omitted, the API defaults to understand . Operation Best for Price per page Extract per page WholeDoc Bench* Parse: text Born-digital PDFs and Office files, no OCR $0.001 $0.007** Not tested Parse: structure OCR for scans with simple layouts, no AI $0.0015 $0.0075 39.4 Parse: understand AI layout analysis: forms, complex layouts $0.009 $0.015 80.8 Parse: agentic Vision language model: cursive, degraded scans, charts $0.018 $0.024 86.2 Classify Zero-shot document labels $0.001 n/a n/a Split Separating merged PDFs into documents $0.003 n/a n/a * WholeDoc Bench parsing score, 5 November 2026; not extraction accuracy. Extract adds $0.006 per page. **API docs list text-mode extract; the agent skill starts at structure. Pricing is in dollars, from 1 balance shared across Nutrient’s cloud APIs, so teams can mix and match. The free plan gives you $5 monthly usage that covers about 330 understand-mode extractions. Starter costs $75 a month for $90 of usage; Growth costs $275 for $345. How does grounded confidence work? In Nutrient’s confidence post , a field scored 0.97 but came from the wrong column. The current score is a composite of optional signals: token probability, candidate margin, grounding and format. Nutrient’s NLI grounding model is open under Apache-2.0. A grounded value can still answer the wrong field. When no score exists, confidence is omitted, not low. Each field also gets a match label: id_match, id_match_multiblock, id_match_partial, fuzzy_match or not_found. Gate on the label first, then confidence. Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser import json, requests API_KEY = "your_api_key" schema = { "type": "object", "properties": { "invoice_number": {"type": "string", "description": "Invoice number below the supplier details."}, "total_amount": {"type": "number", "description": "Printed final total including tax. Not the subtotal."}, }, "required": ["invoice_number", "total_amount"], } instructions = {"schema": schema, "parseConfig": {"mode": "understand"}, "options": {"includeCitations": True}} with open("invoice.pdf", "rb") as f: r = requests.post( "https://api.nutrient.io/extraction/extract", headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}"}, files={"file": ("invoice.pdf", f, "application/pdf"), "instructions": (None, json.dumps(instructions), "application/json")}, timeout=300, ) r.raise_for_status() out = r.json()["output"] data, metadata = out.get("data") or {}, out.get("metadata") or {} EXACT = {"id_match", "id_match_multiblock"} THRESHOLD = 0.97 # illustrative only; evaluate on representative documents for field in schema["properties"]: # loop over expected fields so none skip review value = data.get(field) meta = metadata.get(field) or {} match, conf = meta.get("match"), meta.get("confidence") # None = no score passes = (value is not None and match in EXACT and conf is not None and conf >= THRESHOLD) print(field, value, match, conf, "page", meta.get("pageNumber"), "PASSES_BASIC_CHECKS" if passes else "REVIEW") This demo covers flat schemas only; production needs type and business-rule checks. The 0.97 bar mirrors money fields in Nutrient’s mortgage tutorial . How do classify and split work? A document decision model powers classify and split . Nutrient reports 96.2% split F1 against 63.7% for Typesafe AI’s Jev. How do agents use it? The hosted MCP server needs no API key. Claude Code connects with 1 command: Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser claude mcp add --transport http --scope user nutrient https://mcp.nutrient.io/mcp Claude and Codex also work via OAuth. Default agentic mode costs $0.018 per page to parse. Coding agents can install the document-extraction-api skill with npx skills add pspdfkit-labs/nutrient-skills –skill document-extraction-api. Can it run locally? On the Mac app, documents stay local only with a local model. Fully offline production needs the SDK . How does it score on WholeDoc Bench? Nutrient’s new WholeDoc Bench scores whole documents, not single pages: 480 documents, 30+ languages, 7 areas. Setting Overall Tables Charts Position ¢/page Nutrient Agentic 86.2 87.1 64.5 88.6 1.8 Nutrient Understand 80.8 86.1 35.1 86.4 0.9 Claude Fable 5.1 (high effort) 67.1 84.7 58.9 66.0 17.8 Azure Document Intelligence 65.9 69.4 0 72.5 ≈2.8 GPT-6.1 Sol (medium effort) 62.9 82.8 47.6 49.3 ≈3.1 Extend (performance) 60.5 80.8 40.6 75.2 2.0 Reducto (R-1) 59.9 76.4 38.5 76.4 ≈1.7 LlamaParse Agentic Plus 56.7 89.5 0* 65.4 ≈5.6 AWS Textract 49.9 71.4 0 70.0 1.5 Docling 40.0 63.9 20.2 0 Local Selected rows, WholeDoc leaderboard , 5 November 2026, list prices. *Score still under review. Cross-page continuity is the biggest gap. On 44 documents with page-spanning tables, 15 of 19 settings rarely kept them whole. Nutrient built and ran it, and the main test set is private. The code is Apache-2.0, with a 10-document public sample. Key Takeaways Fields carry pages, regions, match labels and, when available, confidence. Configure and test in Studio before writing any API code. Understand-mode extraction costs $15 per 1,000 pages. Agentic tops Nutrient’s WholeDoc Bench at 86.2 for 1.8¢ per page. Charts remain hard: 64.5 is the best WholeDoc chart score. See the Data Extraction API , benchmarks , MCP server and agent skill on GitHub . content.entityName: New LoRA Adapter Lifts Qwen3.8 Coding Success From 39% to 65%

data.title: New LoRA Adapter Lifts Qwen3.8 Coding Success From 39% to 65%
data.summary: Hugging Face released Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted, an Apache-2.0 LoRA adapter trained with reinforcement learning for the pi coding agent. It lifts SWE-bench Pro hard-51 pass@1 from 39.2% to 64.7% and Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 39.5% to 55.8%. The post New LoRA Adapter Lifts Qwen3.8 Coding Success From 39% to 65% appeared first on MarkTechPost .
data.content: Hugging Face’s harness-hub team has released Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted , a LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B . It was trained with reinforcement learning to work inside the pi coding agent . The Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted LoRA adapter targets one harness instead of general chat. For developers running local coding agents, that is the point. You keep the open base model and swap in a small, harness-specific adapter. TL;DR Size: LoRA rank 32 (alpha 64) on Qwen3.8-27B, a 27B dense hybrid with 262,144 native context. Merged BF16 checkpoint is about 54 GB. Runs on: vLLM with LoRA enabled, or llama.cpp with a GGUF adapter on a Q8_0 base. Inference VRAM is not disclosed. Training used 2x NVIDIA B200. Performance: Large pass@1 gains inside pi with thinking off, plus far shorter sessions. Best: 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), up from 39.2%. Worst: 55.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The base model with thinking already reaches 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro. Bottom line: Best: thinking-level accuracy at about 4.5x fewer tokens. Worst: small eval sets, self-reported, pi only. What is Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted? Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted is a PEFT LoRA adapter that turns Qwen3.8-27B into a model tuned for pi. pi is an MIT-licensed agent toolkit with a coding agent CLI. The adapter is released under Apache-2.0 . It applies to the q, k, v, o, gate, up and down projections. It only works on Qwen3.8-27B. The base model is a dense hybrid . It alternates Gated DeltaNet linear-attention blocks with Gated Attention blocks across 64 layers. How does the harness adapter training work? The method comes from Hugging Face’s harness adapters post from November 6. The idea is 1 LoRA adapter per model and harness. Training runs inside the unmodified harness on verifiable tasks. For this checkpoint, the model card lists these details: Algorithm: AsyncGRPO from TRL , 8 rollouts per task at temperature 0.8. Tasks: 750 scale800 tasks interleaved with 300 TermGrade tasks. Reward: verifier correctness plus a tool-efficiency bonus with weight 0.1. Budget: up to 50 agent steps and 1,800 seconds per rollout, thinking off. Checkpoint: step 160. The run stopped at step 191 of 1,000 planned. Every tool call passes through safeagents , a rule-based proxy. It blocks calls such as fetching benchmark answers from the Hub. Blocked rollouts score 0, so RL pushes the model away from reward hacking. Benchmarks: how much does the LoRA adapter help? All numbers below are self-reported. They use the pi harness, 1 attempt per task. Benchmark (pi, thinking off) Base Qwen3.8-27B pi-adapted Change SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 39.2% 64.7% +25.5 ± 14.2 pts (p = 0.0023) Terminal-Bench 2.1 (86 tasks) 39.5% 55.8% +16.3 ± 9.1 pts (p = 0.0013) The adapter solved 15 new SWE-bench Pro tasks and lost 2. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, it gained 16 and lost 2. Efficiency is the larger story. On tasks both models solved, median turns fell from 59 to 23 on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, they fell from 18 to 8. The adapter also generates about 4.5x fewer tokens than the base model with thinking. && How does it compare with thinking mode and other adapters? With thinking on, the base model already scores 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro and 54.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. So the adapter matches thinking-level accuracy without paying for long reasoning traces. With thinking on, the adapter reaches 66.7% and 56.6%. Feature Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted Qwen3.8-27B base, thinking on Qwen3.8-27B-opencode-adapted bytkim/Qwen3.8-27B-pi Type LoRA r=32 Base model LoRA r=32 Full fine-tune, 28B Method AsyncGRPO RL None AsyncGRPO RL SFT then GRPO Harness pi pi OpenCode pi License Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 64.7% 64.7% 51.0% (OpenCode) Not disclosed Terminal-Bench 2.1 55.8% 54.2% 53.0% (OpenCode) Not disclosed Token use ~4.5x fewer than base + thinking Baseline ~6x to 8x fewer than base + thinking ~41% fewer output tokens (Terminal-Bench) Training hardware 2x B200 Not disclosed 2x B200 Not disclosed OpenCode adapter numbers use a different harness and are not directly comparable. How do you deploy it? The model card gives 4 routes: vLLM: serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B with --enable-lora --max-lora-rank 32 , thinking disabled. Point pi at http://localhost:8000/v1 . llama.cpp: load the GGUF adapter on a Q8_0 base GGUF. Llama.app on macOS: register the adapter with a 32,768-token context. Merge: merge with PEFT on CPU, then serve the 54 GB BF16 result without LoRA flags. Because adapters share 1 base model, a single server can host pi and OpenCode adapters side by side. Key Takeaways Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted is an Apache-2.0, rank-32 RL LoRA for the pi agent. SWE-bench Pro hard-51 rises from 39.2% to 64.7%, thinking off. Median turns drop from 59 to 23 on SWE-bench Pro. It matches base-with-thinking accuracy at about 4.5x fewer tokens. Results are self-reported on small sets; the tweet’s 29.4% baseline was corrected. content.entityName: Uber's Secure AI Framework Governs Autonomous AI Agents across Their Lifecycle

data.title: Uber's Secure AI Framework Governs Autonomous AI Agents across Their Lifecycle
data.summary: In a recent article, Uber Engineering highlights the limitations of traditional identity and API controls in securing AI agents that dynamically reason over external content and take real-world actions. Uber developed a framework to determine whether an agent's action is appropriate given the user's request, the agent's intended purpose, its permissions, and the context of the interaction. By Sergio De Simone

data.title: Anthropic Outlines its AI-Powered Code Review Process for Claude Code
data.summary: Anthropic has outlined how the Claude Code team handles code reviews as AI agents increasingly contribute to its codebase. The approach relies on multiple layers of automated verification, AI-powered reviews, and risk-based human approval, aiming to reduce manual review time without increasing regressions or production incidents. By Robert Krzaczyński
